//! Short-Time Fourier Transform and analytic signal computation.

use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::sync::Arc;

use num_complex::Complex;
use realfft::{RealFftPlanner, RealToComplex};
use rustfft::FftPlanner;

use crate::error::{MusicError, Result};

/// Computes the analytic signal of a real-valued input using the Hilbert transform.
///
/// The analytic signal `z(t) = x(t) + j·H{x(t)}` has a one-sided spectrum; its magnitude is the
/// instantaneous envelope and its argument is the instantaneous phase.
///
/// # Algorithm
/// 1. Forward FFT of the real input.
/// 2. Apply the one-sided spectral window H: `H[0] = 1`, `H[k] = 2` for the positive
///    frequencies `1 ≤ k < (N+1)/2`, `H[N/2] = 1` for the Nyquist bin of even N, and `H = 0` for
///    the negative frequencies `k > N/2` (as in `scipy.signal.hilbert`).
/// 3. Inverse FFT → analytic signal.
///
/// # Examples
/// ```
/// use musicrs::analytic_signal;
/// use std::f64::consts::PI;
/// let n = 256;
/// let cos: Vec<f64> = (0..n).map(|i| (2.0 * PI * 10.0 * i as f64 / n as f64).cos()).collect();
/// let z = analytic_signal(&cos);
/// // Magnitude should be approximately 1 everywhere (after transients settle)
/// for &c in &z[10..n-10] {
///     assert!((c.norm() - 1.0).abs() < 0.01);
/// }
/// ```
pub fn analytic_signal(data: &[f64]) -> Vec<Complex<f64>> {
    analytic_signal_with(data, &mut FftPlanner::new())
}

/// [`analytic_signal`] with a caller-owned planner, so that several signals of the same
/// length (one per channel) share its cached FFT plans instead of rebuilding them.
pub(crate) fn analytic_signal_with(
    data: &[f64],
    planner: &mut FftPlanner<f64>,
) -> Vec<Complex<f64>> {
    let n = data.len();
    if n == 0 {
        return Vec::new();
    }

    // Forward FFT
    let fft_forward = planner.plan_fft_forward(n);
    let mut spectrum: Vec<Complex<f64>> = data.iter().map(|&x| Complex::new(x, 0.0)).collect();
    fft_forward.process(&mut spectrum);

    // One-sided spectral window. DC is unchanged; so is the Nyquist bin N/2, which only
    // exists for even N. Odd N has no Nyquist bin: bin (N-1)/2 is a positive frequency.
    for sample in &mut spectrum[1..n.div_ceil(2)] {
        *sample *= 2.0;
    }
    for sample in &mut spectrum[n / 2 + 1..] {
        *sample = Complex::new(0.0, 0.0);
    }

    // Inverse FFT
    let fft_inverse = planner.plan_fft_inverse(n);
    fft_inverse.process(&mut spectrum);

    // Normalise
    let norm = n as f64;
    spectrum.iter().map(|c| c / norm).collect()
}

/// How many real FFT plans [`real_fft_plan`] keeps per thread.
const REAL_PLAN_CACHE_SIZE: usize = 4;

thread_local! {
    /// The most recently used real forward FFT plans of this thread, most recent last.
    static REAL_PLANS: RefCell<Vec<Arc<dyn RealToComplex<f64>>>> = const { RefCell::new(Vec::new()) };
}

/// A real forward FFT plan of length `n`, reused across calls on the same thread.
///
/// Planning a long transform (and computing its twiddle factors) costs about as much as
/// running it a few times, and repeated calls on recordings of one length are the common
/// case. Only the last [`REAL_PLAN_CACHE_SIZE`] lengths are kept, so that a stream of
/// different lengths does not keep every plan alive.
///
/// Each thread that calls this keeps its plans (their twiddle factors take memory
/// proportional to the transform length) until the thread exits. With
/// many long-lived threads on long recordings, that is up to
/// [`REAL_PLAN_CACHE_SIZE`] plans per thread.
pub(crate) fn real_fft_plan(n: usize) -> Arc<dyn RealToComplex<f64>> {
    REAL_PLANS.with(|cache| {
        let mut cache = cache.borrow_mut();
        let plan = match cache.iter().position(|p| p.len() == n) {
            Some(i) => cache.remove(i),
            None => {
                if cache.len() == REAL_PLAN_CACHE_SIZE {
                    cache.remove(0);
                }
                RealFftPlanner::<f64>::new().plan_fft_forward(n)
            }
        };
        cache.push(Arc::clone(&plan));
        plan
    })
}

/// Computes the Short-Time Fourier Transform of a real-valued signal.
///
/// Returns a matrix of shape `[freq_bins][num_windows]` where
/// `freq_bins = nfft / 2 + 1` (single-sided spectrum via real FFT).
///
/// # Arguments
/// * `data`       – Real-valued input samples.
/// * `nfft`       – Window (FFT) size.
/// * `no_overlap` – Number of samples shared between consecutive windows.
///
/// # Errors
/// [`MusicError::InvalidNfft`] if `nfft` is 0, [`MusicError::InvalidOverlap`] if
/// `no_overlap >= nfft`, then [`MusicError::DataShorterThanWindow`] if `data` is shorter
/// than `nfft`. The data length is checked before the FFT is planned, so memory stays bounded
/// by the input size whatever `nfft` is.
///
/// # Examples
/// ```
/// use musicrs::stft;
/// use std::f64::consts::PI;
/// let n = 512;
/// let freq_bin = 16usize;
/// let sr = 512.0_f64;
/// let sine: Vec<f64> = (0..n)
///     .map(|i| (2.0 * PI * freq_bin as f64 * i as f64 / sr).sin())
///     .collect();
/// let result = stft(&sine, 64, 0)?;
/// assert_eq!(result.len(), 64 / 2 + 1); // bins 0..=32
/// assert_eq!(result[0].len(), 512 / 64); // non-overlapping windows
/// // 16 cycles per 512 samples is 2 cycles per 64-sample window: bin 2 in every window
/// for w in 0..result[0].len() {
///     let peak = (0..result.len())
///         .max_by(|&a, &b| result[a][w].norm().total_cmp(&result[b][w].norm()))
///         .unwrap();
///     assert_eq!(peak, 2);
/// }
/// # Ok::<(), musicrs::MusicError>(())
/// ```
pub fn stft(data: &[f64], nfft: usize, no_overlap: usize) -> Result<Vec<Vec<Complex<f64>>>> {
    stft_with(data, nfft, no_overlap, &mut FftPlanner::new())
}

/// [`stft`] with a caller-owned planner, so that several signals (one per channel) share
/// its cached FFT plan instead of rebuilding it.
pub(crate) fn stft_with(
    data: &[f64],
    nfft: usize,
    no_overlap: usize,
    planner: &mut FftPlanner<f64>,
) -> Result<Vec<Vec<Complex<f64>>>> {
    if nfft == 0 {
        return Err(MusicError::InvalidNfft);
    }
    if no_overlap >= nfft {
        return Err(MusicError::InvalidOverlap { no_overlap, nfft });
    }
    if data.len() < nfft {
        // Planning the FFT and allocating the bins are O(nfft): return before either.
        return Err(MusicError::DataShorterThanWindow {
            nfft,
            samples: data.len(),
        });
    }

    let step = nfft - no_overlap;
    let freq_bins = nfft / 2 + 1;
    // Use real-to-complex FFT plan (standard forward FFT on real-padded input)
    let fft = planner.plan_fft_forward(nfft);

    let num_windows = (data.len() - nfft) / step + 1;

    // result[freq_bin][window_index]
    let mut result: Vec<Vec<Complex<f64>>> =
        vec![vec![Complex::new(0.0, 0.0); num_windows]; freq_bins];

    for (win_idx, start) in (0..).zip((0..).step_by(step).take(num_windows)) {
        let end = start + nfft;
        let mut buf: Vec<Complex<f64>> = data[start..end]
            .iter()
            .map(|&x| Complex::new(x, 0.0))
            .collect();
        fft.process(&mut buf);
        for bin in 0..freq_bins {
            result[bin][win_idx] = buf[bin];
        }
    }

    Ok(result)
}

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    use approx::assert_abs_diff_eq;
    use std::f64::consts::PI;

    /// Pure cosine → analytic signal magnitude ≈ 1 (away from edges).
    #[test]
    fn analytic_signal_cosine_magnitude() {
        let n = 256usize;
        let f0 = 10.0_f64;
        let data: Vec<f64> = (0..n)
            .map(|i| (2.0 * PI * f0 * i as f64 / n as f64).cos())
            .collect();
        let z = analytic_signal(&data);
        // Skip 10 samples at each edge where Gibbs artefacts may occur
        for c in &z[10..n - 10] {
            assert_abs_diff_eq!(c.norm(), 1.0, epsilon = 0.02);
        }
    }

    /// Analytic signal of a cosine has imaginary part ≈ -sine (shifted by -π/2).
    #[test]
    fn analytic_signal_imag_is_negative_sine() {
        let n = 256usize;
        let f0 = 8.0_f64;
        let data: Vec<f64> = (0..n)
            .map(|i| (2.0 * PI * f0 * i as f64 / n as f64).cos())
            .collect();
        let z = analytic_signal(&data);
        for (i, zi) in z.iter().enumerate().take(n - 10).skip(10) {
            // H{cos(ωt)} = +sin(ωt), so z(t) = cos(ωt) + i·sin(ωt)
            let expected_imag = (2.0 * PI * f0 * i as f64 / n as f64).sin();
            assert_abs_diff_eq!(zi.im, expected_imag, epsilon = 0.02);
        }
    }

    /// Deterministic pseudo-random samples in [-1, 1) (LCG).
    fn noise(n: usize, seed: u64) -> Vec<f64> {
        let mut state = seed;
        (0..n)
            .map(|_| {
                state = state
                    .wrapping_mul(6_364_136_223_846_793_005)
                    .wrapping_add(1_442_695_040_888_963_407);
                2.0 * (state >> 11) as f64 / (1u64 << 53) as f64 - 1.0
            })
            .collect()
    }

    /// The real part of the analytic signal is the input itself, for even and odd lengths.
    #[test]
    fn analytic_signal_real_part_is_input() {
        for n in [1, 2, 7, 64, 255] {
            let x = noise(n, n as u64);
            let z = analytic_signal(&x);
            assert_eq!(z.len(), n);
            for (zi, xi) in z.iter().zip(&x) {
                assert_abs_diff_eq!(zi.re, *xi, epsilon = 1e-12);
            }
        }
    }

    /// The analytic signal has no negative-frequency content, for even and odd lengths.
    #[test]
    fn analytic_signal_is_one_sided() {
        for n in [8, 9, 64, 255] {
            let mut z = analytic_signal(&noise(n, 1 + n as u64));
            FftPlanner::<f64>::new().plan_fft_forward(n).process(&mut z);
            for (k, c) in z.iter().enumerate().skip(n / 2 + 1) {
                assert!(
                    c.norm() < 1e-9,
                    "n = {n}: bin {k} has magnitude {}",
                    c.norm()
                );
            }
        }
    }

    /// A planner reused across signals gives bit-identical results to a fresh one per call.
    #[test]
    fn shared_planner_matches_fresh_planner() {
        let mut planner = FftPlanner::new();
        for seed in 0..3 {
            let x = noise(255, 100 + seed);
            assert_eq!(analytic_signal_with(&x, &mut planner), analytic_signal(&x));
            assert_eq!(
                stft_with(&x, 32, 8, &mut planner),
                stft(&x, 32, 8),
                "seed {seed}"
            );
        }
    }

    #[test]
    fn analytic_signal_empty_input() {
        assert!(analytic_signal(&[]).is_empty());
    }

    /// STFT column count matches expected number of windows.
    #[test]
    fn stft_window_count() {
        let data = vec![0.0f64; 100];
        let nfft = 16;
        let overlap = 8;
        let step = nfft - overlap; // 8
        let expected_windows = (data.len() - nfft) / step + 1; // (100 - 16) / 8 + 1 = 11
        let result = stft(&data, nfft, overlap).unwrap();
        assert_eq!(result[0].len(), expected_windows);
    }

    #[test]
    fn stft_rejects_zero_nfft() {
        assert_eq!(stft(&[0.0; 8], 0, 0), Err(MusicError::InvalidNfft));
    }

    #[test]
    fn stft_rejects_overlap_of_whole_window() {
        assert_eq!(
            stft(&[0.0; 8], 4, 4),
            Err(MusicError::InvalidOverlap {
                no_overlap: 4,
                nfft: 4
            })
        );
    }

    /// Data shorter than one window is an error, returned before the O(nfft) FFT plan and
    /// bins are allocated: a huge `nfft` must not abort the process.
    #[test]
    fn stft_rejects_data_shorter_than_window() {
        assert_eq!(
            stft(&[0.0; 4], 1 << 40, 0),
            Err(MusicError::DataShorterThanWindow {
                nfft: 1 << 40,
                samples: 4
            })
        );
        assert_eq!(
            stft(&[], 2, 1),
            Err(MusicError::DataShorterThanWindow {
                nfft: 2,
                samples: 0
            })
        );
        // Parameter errors come first.
        assert_eq!(
            stft(&[0.0; 4], 1 << 40, 1 << 40),
            Err(MusicError::InvalidOverlap {
                no_overlap: 1 << 40,
                nfft: 1 << 40
            })
        );
    }

    /// With overlap, window w starts at sample w·(nfft − no_overlap): its DC bin is the sum
    /// of exactly those samples.
    #[test]
    fn stft_overlapping_windows_start_at_step() {
        let data: Vec<f64> = (0..20).map(f64::from).collect();
        let (nfft, overlap) = (8, 5);
        let result = stft(&data, nfft, overlap).unwrap();
        assert_eq!(result[0].len(), 5); // (20 − 8) / 3 + 1
        for (w, dc) in result[0].iter().enumerate() {
            let start = w * (nfft - overlap);
            let expected: f64 = data[start..start + nfft].iter().sum();
            assert_abs_diff_eq!(dc.re, expected, epsilon = 1e-9);
            assert_abs_diff_eq!(dc.im, 0.0, epsilon = 1e-9);
        }
    }

    /// STFT freq_bins = nfft/2 + 1.
    #[test]
    fn stft_freq_bins() {
        let data = vec![0.0f64; 64];
        let nfft = 32;
        let result = stft(&data, nfft, 0).unwrap();
        assert_eq!(result.len(), nfft / 2 + 1);
    }

    /// STFT of a pure sine wave has a peak at the expected frequency bin.
    #[test]
    fn stft_peak_at_correct_bin() {
        let nfft = 64usize;
        let target_bin = 4usize; // frequency = target_bin * (sr / nfft)
        // Generate enough samples for several non-overlapping windows
        let n = nfft * 8;
        let data: Vec<f64> = (0..n)
            .map(|i| (2.0 * PI * target_bin as f64 * i as f64 / nfft as f64).sin())
            .collect();
        let result = stft(&data, nfft, 0).unwrap();
        // In each window, bin `target_bin` should dominate
        for win in 0..result[0].len() {
            let peak_bin = (0..result.len())
                .max_by(|&a, &b| {
                    result[a][win]
                        .norm()
                        .partial_cmp(&result[b][win].norm())
                        .unwrap()
                })
                .unwrap();
            assert_eq!(peak_bin, target_bin);
        }
    }

    /// The plan cache returns the cached plan for a repeated length, keeps at most
    /// `REAL_PLAN_CACHE_SIZE` lengths and evicts the least recently used one.
    #[test]
    fn real_fft_plan_cache_reuses_and_evicts() {
        // Runs on its own test thread, so the thread-local cache starts empty
        let lengths: Vec<usize> = (1..=REAL_PLAN_CACHE_SIZE).map(|i| 100 + i).collect();
        let first: Vec<_> = lengths.iter().map(|&n| real_fft_plan(n)).collect();
        // Every length is cached: the same plan comes back
        for (n, plan) in lengths.iter().zip(&first) {
            assert!(
                Arc::ptr_eq(&real_fft_plan(*n), plan),
                "length {n} not reused"
            );
        }
        // Touch the first length so the second becomes the least recently used, then add one
        assert!(Arc::ptr_eq(&real_fft_plan(lengths[0]), &first[0]));
        real_fft_plan(999);
        let cached: Vec<usize> = REAL_PLANS.with(|c| c.borrow().iter().map(|p| p.len()).collect());
        assert_eq!(cached.len(), REAL_PLAN_CACHE_SIZE);
        assert!(
            !cached.contains(&lengths[1]),
            "least recently used length kept: {cached:?}"
        );
        assert!(cached.contains(&lengths[0]) && cached.contains(&999));
        assert_eq!(real_fft_plan(37).len(), 37);
    }

//! Short-Time Fourier Transform and analytic signal computation.

use std::cell::RefCell;
use std::sync::Arc;

use num_complex::Complex;
use realfft::{RealFftPlanner, RealToComplex};
use rustfft::FftPlanner;

use crate::error::{MusicError, Result};

/// Computes the analytic signal of a real-valued input using the Hilbert transform.
///
/// The analytic signal `z(t) = x(t) + j·H{x(t)}` has a one-sided spectrum; its magnitude is the
/// instantaneous envelope and its argument is the instantaneous phase.
///
/// # Algorithm
/// 1. Forward FFT of the real input.
/// 2. Apply the one-sided spectral window H: `H[0] = 1`, `H[k] = 2` for the positive
///    frequencies `1 ≤ k < (N+1)/2`, `H[N/2] = 1` for the Nyquist bin of even N, and `H = 0` for
///    the negative frequencies `k > N/2` (as in `scipy.signal.hilbert`).
/// 3. Inverse FFT → analytic signal.
///
/// # Examples
/// ```
/// use musicrs::analytic_signal;
/// use std::f64::consts::PI;
/// let n = 256;
/// let cos: Vec<f64> = (0..n).map(|i| (2.0 * PI * 10.0 * i as f64 / n as f64).cos()).collect();
/// let z = analytic_signal(&cos);
/// // Magnitude should be approximately 1 everywhere (after transients settle)
/// for &c in &z[10..n-10] {
///     assert!((c.norm() - 1.0).abs() < 0.01);
/// }
/// ```
pub fn analytic_signal(data: &[f64]) -> Vec<Complex<f64>> {
    analytic_signal_with(data, &mut FftPlanner::new())
}

/// [`analytic_signal`] with a caller-owned planner, so that several signals of the same
/// length (one per channel) share its cached FFT plans instead of rebuilding them.
pub(crate) fn analytic_signal_with(
    data: &[f64],
    planner: &mut FftPlanner<f64>,
) -> Vec<Complex<f64>> {
    let n = data.len();
    if n == 0 {
        return Vec::new();
    }

    // Forward FFT
    let fft_forward = planner.plan_fft_forward(n);
    let mut spectrum: Vec<Complex<f64>> = data.iter().map(|&x| Complex::new(x, 0.0)).collect();
    fft_forward.process(&mut spectrum);

    // One-sided spectral window. DC is unchanged; so is the Nyquist bin N/2, which only
    // exists for even N. Odd N has no Nyquist bin: bin (N-1)/2 is a positive frequency.
    for sample in &mut spectrum[1..n.div_ceil(2)] {
        *sample *= 2.0;
    }
    for sample in &mut spectrum[n / 2 + 1..] {
        *sample = Complex::new(0.0, 0.0);
    }

    // Inverse FFT
    let fft_inverse = planner.plan_fft_inverse(n);
    fft_inverse.process(&mut spectrum);

    // Normalise
    let norm = n as f64;
    spectrum.iter().map(|c| c / norm).collect()
}

/// How many real FFT plans [`real_fft_plan`] keeps per thread.
const REAL_PLAN_CACHE_SIZE: usize = 4;

thread_local! {
    /// The most recently used real forward FFT plans of this thread, most recent last.
    static REAL_PLANS: RefCell<Vec<Arc<dyn RealToComplex<f64>>>> = const { RefCell::new(Vec::new()) };
}

/// A real forward FFT plan of length `n`, reused across calls on the same thread.
///
/// Planning a long transform (and computing its twiddle factors) costs about as much as
/// running it a few times, and repeated calls on recordings of one length are the common
/// case. Only the last [`REAL_PLAN_CACHE_SIZE`] lengths are kept, so that a stream of
/// different lengths does not keep every plan alive.
///
/// Each thread that calls this keeps its plans (their twiddle factors take memory
/// proportional to the transform length) until the thread exits. With
/// many long-lived threads on long recordings, that is up to
/// [`REAL_PLAN_CACHE_SIZE`] plans per thread.
pub(crate) fn real_fft_plan(n: usize) -> Arc<dyn RealToComplex<f64>> {
    REAL_PLANS.with(|cache| {
        let mut cache = cache.borrow_mut();
        let plan = match cache.iter().position(|p| p.len() == n) {
            Some(i) => cache.remove(i),
            None => {
                if cache.len() == REAL_PLAN_CACHE_SIZE {
                    cache.remove(0);
                }
                RealFftPlanner::<f64>::new().plan_fft_forward(n)
            }
        };
        cache.push(Arc::clone(&plan));
        plan
    })
}

/// Computes the Short-Time Fourier Transform of a real-valued signal.
///
/// Returns a matrix of shape `[freq_bins][num_windows]` where
/// `freq_bins = nfft / 2 + 1` (single-sided spectrum via real FFT).
///
/// # Arguments
/// * `data`       – Real-valued input samples.
/// * `nfft`       – Window (FFT) size.
/// * `no_overlap` – Number of samples shared between consecutive windows.
///
/// # Errors
/// [`MusicError::InvalidNfft`] if `nfft` is 0, [`MusicError::InvalidOverlap`] if
/// `no_overlap >= nfft`, then [`MusicError::DataShorterThanWindow`] if `data` is shorter
/// than `nfft`. The data length is checked before the FFT is planned, so memory stays bounded
/// by the input size whatever `nfft` is.
///
/// # Examples
/// ```
/// use musicrs::stft;
/// use std::f64::consts::PI;
/// let n = 512;
/// let freq_bin = 16usize;
/// let sr = 512.0_f64;
/// let sine: Vec<f64> = (0..n)
///     .map(|i| (2.0 * PI * freq_bin as f64 * i as f64 / sr).sin())
///     .collect();
/// let result = stft(&sine, 64, 0)?;
/// assert_eq!(result.len(), 64 / 2 + 1); // bins 0..=32
/// assert_eq!(result[0].len(), 512 / 64); // non-overlapping windows
/// // 16 cycles per 512 samples is 2 cycles per 64-sample window: bin 2 in every window
/// for w in 0..result[0].len() {
///     let peak = (0..result.len())
///         .max_by(|&a, &b| result[a][w].norm().total_cmp(&result[b][w].norm()))
///         .unwrap();
///     assert_eq!(peak, 2);
/// }
/// # Ok::<(), musicrs::MusicError>(())
/// ```
pub fn stft(data: &[f64], nfft: usize, no_overlap: usize) -> Result<Vec<Vec<Complex<f64>>>> {
    stft_with(data, nfft, no_overlap, &mut FftPlanner::new())
}

/// [`stft`] with a caller-owned planner, so that several signals (one per channel) share
/// its cached FFT plan instead of rebuilding it.
pub(crate) fn stft_with(
    data: &[f64],
    nfft: usize,
    no_overlap: usize,
    planner: &mut FftPlanner<f64>,
) -> Result<Vec<Vec<Complex<f64>>>> {
    if nfft == 0 {
        return Err(MusicError::InvalidNfft);
    }
    if no_overlap >= nfft {
        return Err(MusicError::InvalidOverlap { no_overlap, nfft });
    }
    if data.len() < nfft {
        // Planning the FFT and allocating the bins are O(nfft): return before either.
        return Err(MusicError::DataShorterThanWindow {
            nfft,
            samples: data.len(),
        });
    }

    let step = nfft - no_overlap;
    let freq_bins = nfft / 2 + 1;
    // Use real-to-complex FFT plan (standard forward FFT on real-padded input)
    let fft = planner.plan_fft_forward(nfft);

    let num_windows = (data.len() - nfft) / step + 1;

    // result[freq_bin][window_index]
    let mut result: Vec<Vec<Complex<f64>>> =
        vec![vec![Complex::new(0.0, 0.0); num_windows]; freq_bins];

    for (win_idx, start) in (0..).zip((0..).step_by(step).take(num_windows)) {
        let end = start + nfft;
        let mut buf: Vec<Complex<f64>> = data[start..end]
            .iter()
            .map(|&x| Complex::new(x, 0.0))
            .collect();
        fft.process(&mut buf);
        for bin in 0..freq_bins {
            result[bin][win_idx] = buf[bin];
        }
    }

    Ok(result)
}

    use super::*;

    /// Pure cosine → analytic signal magnitude ≈ 1 (away from edges).
    #[test]
    fn analytic_signal_cosine_magnitude() {
        let n = 256usize;
        let f0 = 10.0_f64;
        let data: Vec<f64> = (0..n)
            .map(|i| (2.0 * PI * f0 * i as f64 / n as f64).cos())
            .collect();
        let z = analytic_signal(&data);
        // Skip 10 samples at each edge where Gibbs artefacts may occur
        for c in &z[10..n - 10] {
            assert_abs_diff_eq!(c.norm(), 1.0, epsilon = 0.02);
        }
    }

    /// Analytic signal of a cosine has imaginary part ≈ -sine (shifted by -π/2).
    #[test]
    fn analytic_signal_imag_is_negative_sine() {
        let n = 256usize;
        let f0 = 8.0_f64;
        let data: Vec<f64> = (0..n)
            .map(|i| (2.0 * PI * f0 * i as f64 / n as f64).cos())
            .collect();
        let z = analytic_signal(&data);
        for (i, zi) in z.iter().enumerate().take(n - 10).skip(10) {
            // H{cos(ωt)} = +sin(ωt), so z(t) = cos(ωt) + i·sin(ωt)
            let expected_imag = (2.0 * PI * f0 * i as f64 / n as f64).sin();
            assert_abs_diff_eq!(zi.im, expected_imag, epsilon = 0.02);
        }
    }

    /// Deterministic pseudo-random samples in [-1, 1) (LCG).
    fn noise(n: usize, seed: u64) -> Vec<f64> {
        let mut state = seed;
        (0..n)
            .map(|_| {
                state = state
                    .wrapping_mul(6_364_136_223_846_793_005)
                    .wrapping_add(1_442_695_040_888_963_407);
                2.0 * (state >> 11) as f64 / (1u64 << 53) as f64 - 1.0
            })
            .collect()
    }

    /// The real part of the analytic signal is the input itself, for even and odd lengths.
    #[test]
    fn analytic_signal_real_part_is_input() {
        for n in [1, 2, 7, 64, 255] {
            let x = noise(n, n as u64);
            let z = analytic_signal(&x);
            assert_eq!(z.len(), n);
            for (zi, xi) in z.iter().zip(&x) {
                assert_abs_diff_eq!(zi.re, *xi, epsilon = 1e-12);
            }
        }
    }

    /// The analytic signal has no negative-frequency content, for even and odd lengths.
    #[test]
    fn analytic_signal_is_one_sided() {
        for n in [8, 9, 64, 255] {
            let mut z = analytic_signal(&noise(n, 1 + n as u64));
            FftPlanner::<f64>::new().plan_fft_forward(n).process(&mut z);
            for (k, c) in z.iter().enumerate().skip(n / 2 + 1) {
                assert!(
                    c.norm() < 1e-9,
                    "n = {n}: bin {k} has magnitude {}",
                    c.norm()
                );
            }
        }
    }

    /// A planner reused across signals gives bit-identical results to a fresh one per call.
    #[test]
    fn shared_planner_matches_fresh_planner() {
        let mut planner = FftPlanner::new();
        for seed in 0..3 {
            let x = noise(255, 100 + seed);
            assert_eq!(analytic_signal_with(&x, &mut planner), analytic_signal(&x));
            assert_eq!(
                stft_with(&x, 32, 8, &mut planner),
                stft(&x, 32, 8),
                "seed {seed}"
            );
        }
    }

            })

    #[test]
    fn stft_rejects_data_shorter_than_window() {
        assert_eq!(
            stft(&[0.0; 4], 1 << 40, 0),
            Err(MusicError::DataShorterThanWindow {
                nfft: 1 << 40,
                samples: 4
            })
        );

                nfft: 2,
                samples: 0
            })

        assert_eq!(
            stft(&[0.0; 4], 1 << 40, 1 << 40),
            Err(MusicError::InvalidOverlap {
                no_overlap: 1 << 40,
                nfft: 1 << 40
            })
        );

    /// of exactly those samples.

    fn stft_overlapping_windows_start_at_step() {
        let data: Vec<f64> = (0..20).map(f64::from).collect();
        let (nfft, overlap) = (8, 5);
        let result = stft(&data, nfft, overlap).unwrap();
        assert_eq!(result[0].len(), 5); // (20 − 8) / 3 + 1
        for (w, dc) in result[0].iter().enumerate() {
            let start = w * (nfft - overlap);
            let expected: f64 = data[start..start + nfft].iter().sum();

        let data = vec![0.0f64; 64];

        assert_eq!(result.len(), nfft / 2 + 1);

    #[test]

        let nfft = 64usize;

        // Generate enough samples for several non-overlapping windows
        let n = nfft * 8;

            .collect();

        for win in 0..result[0].len() {

                        .partial_cmp(&result[b][win].norm())

    /// `REAL_PLAN_CACHE_SIZE` lengths and evicts the least recently used one.
    #[test]
    fn real_fft_plan_cache_reuses_and_evicts() {

        let lengths: Vec<usize> = (1..=REAL_PLAN_CACHE_SIZE).map(|i| 100 + i).collect();
        let first: Vec<_> = lengths.iter().map(|&n| real_fft_plan(n)).collect();
        // Every length is cached: the same plan comes back
        for (n, plan) in lengths.iter().zip(&first) {
            assert!(
                Arc::ptr_eq(&real_fft_plan(*n), plan),
                "length {n} not reused"
            );
        }

        assert!(Arc::ptr_eq(&real_fft_plan(lengths[0]), &first[0]));

        assert_eq!(cached.len(), REAL_PLAN_CACHE_SIZE);
        assert!(
            !cached.contains(&lengths[1]),
            "least recently used length kept: {cached:?}"
        );
        assert!(cached.contains(&lengths[0]) && cached.contains(&999));
        assert_eq!(real_fft_plan(37).len(), 37);
    }

        n_sources: usize,
        bins: Option<&[usize]>,

        let freq_bins = nfft / 2 + 1;

        let default_bins: Vec<usize> = (1..freq_bins).collect();
        let mut active_bins: Vec<usize> = bins
            .unwrap_or(&default_bins)
            .iter()
            .copied()
            .filter(|bin| (1..freq_bins).contains(bin))
            .collect();
        // A repeated bin would count more than once in the geometric mean; the order of the
        // bins does not change the mean.
        active_bins.sort_unstable();
        active_bins.dedup();
        if active_bins.is_empty() {
            return Err(MusicError::NoUsableBins);
        }

        // STFT per microphone channel, all sharing one FFT plan
        let mut planner = FftPlanner::new();
        let stfts: Vec<Vec<Vec<Cplx>>> = (0..n_mics)
            .map(|m| {
                let row: Vec<f64> = data.row(m).iter().copied().collect();
                stft_with(&row, nfft, 0, &mut planner)
            })
            .collect::<Result<_>>()?;
        let n_windows = stfts[0][0].len();

        // Geometric mean, accumulated as a sum of logarithms: the product of hundreds of
        // per-bin spectra overflows f64.
        let mut log_sum: Option<Vec<f64>> = None;
        let mut angles_out: Vec<f64> = Vec::new();
        let mut n_processed = 0usize;

        // Silence is judged against the strongest bin of the whole spectrum, DC included,
        // so that a requested bin holding only rounding residue is still recognised.
        let strongest = stfts
            .iter()
            .fold(vec![0.0; freq_bins], |mut power, mic| {
                for (p, bin) in power.iter_mut().zip(mic) {
                    *p += bin.iter().map(|c| c.norm_sqr()).sum::<f64>() / n_windows as f64;
                }
                power
            })
            .into_iter()
            .fold(0.0, f64::max);

        for bin in active_bins {
            // Cross-spectral matrix of this bin, averaged over time windows. Built one bin
            // at a time so that only one n_mics x n_mics matrix is alive at once.
            let bin_slices: Vec<&[Cplx]> = stfts.iter().map(|s| s[bin].as_slice()).collect();
            let mut cov = CMatrix::zeros(n_mics, n_mics);
            for col in
                (0..n_windows).map(|w| CVec::from_iterator(n_mics, bin_slices.iter().map(|s| s[w])))

            if cov.trace().re <= SILENCE_RATIO * strongest {

                    angles_out = angles;

                }

            n_processed += 1;
        }

        let merged: Vec<f64> = sum
            .iter()
            .map(|&v| (v / n_processed as f64).exp())
            .collect();

    }

/// A power of two close to `max_abs`, the largest absolute value in some data, to divide
/// the data by. MUSIC does not depend on the data's scale, and dividing by a power of two
/// is exact, so this changes no result: it only keeps the sums of squares in the
/// covariance and energy from overflowing for very loud data (or underflowing for very
/// quiet data).
fn power_of_two_scale(max_abs: f64) -> f64 {
    if max_abs > 0.0 {
        2f64.powi((max_abs.log2().floor() as i32).clamp(-1000, 1000))
    } else {
        1.0
    }
}

/// `data` divided by [`power_of_two_scale`] of its largest absolute value.
fn normalised_real(data: &DMatrix<f64>) -> DMatrix<f64> {
    data / power_of_two_scale(data.amax())
}

/// The mean of `values`, summed with Neumaier's compensated summation so that it is
/// correct to about one ulp: subtracting it from constant data then leaves (almost)
/// nothing, which [`SILENCE_RATIO`] relies on. With a plain sum, 16000 samples of 0.3
/// leave a residue above the threshold.
fn accurate_mean<'a>(values: impl ExactSizeIterator<Item = &'a f64>) -> f64 {
    let n = values.len() as f64;

lastPrompt: So tell me, why is the vectorized IFB MUSIC implementation in python still faster?

content.text:
**Short answer:** with one bin, almost none of the time goes into MUSIC. About 85% of a musicrs call is preprocessing that grows with recording length, and numpy does that part in fewer passes and in vectorized C. musicrs makes several slow scalar passes over the 64 000 samples before it reaches the one bin it was asked for.

The benchmark agrees. Going from the 1 s to the 2 s recording adds about 1 ms to musicrs (1.17 → 2.15 ms) but only about 0.37 ms to numpy (0.55 → 0.92 ms). The fixed part is about the same for both, roughly 0.17 ms. So the whole gap is in the work done per sample.

## Where a musicrs call spends its time (1 s recording, one bin, about 1.09 ms)

I timed each step of `ifb_music_spectrum` (`src/music.rs:847`) on its own, in a separate crate in the scratchpad. The repo is unchanged.

| Step | µs | What's slow about it |
|---|---:|---|
| `check_real_samples`: NaN check and largest absolute value | ~150 | `max` over `f64` is one long chain where each step waits for the last, so it doesn't vectorize (about 2.4 ns per sample) |
| `normalised_real`: `data.amax()` again, then divide into a new matrix | ~320 | **Computes the same maximum a second time.** `check_real_samples` already returns it, but `ifb_music_spectrum` throws it away |
| Copying each channel out with `data.row(m).iter()` | ~130 | nalgebra's row iterator is slow; reading the slice with a stride takes ~40 |
| `stft_with` on 4 channels | ~380 | Complex FFT on real input, a new `Vec` for every window, results copied into a `Vec<Vec>` |
| Power per bin to find the strongest (used by the silence check) | ~27 | |
| Covariance, eigendecomposition | ~10 | |
| `spectrum` for 720 angles, plus `ln`/`exp` | ~115 | The actual MUSIC work |

numpy has no input check and no scaling. Its `reshape` doesn't copy anything, and it runs one batched real FFT in C (`np.fft.rfft`) before reading bin 14. That leaves about 550 µs, mostly spent on the STFT and the vectorized spectrum.

**Why musicrs wins with 80 bins (3.9×):** that preprocessing is paid once per call. Each extra bin costs musicrs about 40 µs. Each extra bin costs numpy about 230 µs, mostly Python per-iteration overhead, `np.linalg.eig` and temporary arrays.

## What would close the gap

None of these change any result; the scaling is by a power of two, which is exact.
1. **Reuse the maximum from `check_real_samples`** in `power_of_two_scale` instead of calling `data.amax()` again: about −150 µs.
2. **Make that loop vectorizable**, for example with several independent maximums combined at the end: most of the remaining ~150 µs.
3. **Scale and split the channels in one pass** over `data.as_slice()`: about −100 µs or more.
4. **Use a real FFT in the STFT** with reused buffers. `realfft` is already a dependency and `real_fft_plan` exists. In my test, the FFTs alone dropped from 270 to 150 µs, with no allocation per window.

Together I'd estimate one bin goes from about 1.1 ms to about 0.35–0.45 ms, which would beat numpy. I haven't measured that yet. It would also cut the fixed cost of the 80-bin case and of narrowband, which uses the same input check.

Want me to write this up as a plan for a `fix/ifb-preprocessing` branch?

Compute the STFT with a real FFT and reused buffers

stft ran a complex FFT on real input and allocated a new buffer for
every window. It now uses the cached real-to-complex plan
(real_fft_plan), which returns bins 0..=nfft/2 directly at about half
the cost, with one input, output and scratch buffer for all windows.
stft_with and its planner parameter are gone: the plan cache is shared.

A new test checks every column against the complex FFT of its window
for even and odd nfft, with and without overlap.

input.content:
Build IFB cross-spectral matrices without per-window allocations

The cross-spectral matrix of each bin was summed as outer products of
nalgebra vectors, allocating a vector, its adjoint and a 4x4 product for
every window: about 8 us per bin, most of it allocation. Each entry of
the lower triangle is now summed over the windows directly, in the same
order, and mirrored into the upper triangle.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

content.text:
A one-bin IFB call now takes about half the time: 1.12 ms → 0.53 ms on the 1 s recording. That brings it level with the numpy baseline (0.55 ms) rather than clearly ahead. The work is three commits on `fix/ifb-preprocessing`; all tests pass and no result changed.

| Commit | Change |
|---|---|
| `26d068e` | Reuses the maximum that `check_real_samples` already computes, instead of calling `data.amax()` again. That loop is now written so the compiler can vectorize it. A new `scaled_rows` scales the data and splits it into channels in one pass; narrowband, IFB and `select_bins_by_energy` all use it. |
| `c048b47` | The STFT uses the cached real FFT (`real_fft_plan`) and reuses its buffers instead of allocating one per window. `stft_with` and its planner parameter are gone. |
| `51e7277` | Each bin's covariance matrix is summed directly, without allocating vectors and a 4×4 matrix for every window. |

## Testing

- **Full suite after each commit:** `cargo test -- --include-ignored` passed after each one, including the slow tests, the golden tests and the doc tests, along with `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check`.
- **New tests:**
  - NaN, +inf and −inf are caught wherever they sit in the data, including in the leftover samples the vectorized loop handles separately, and the maximum is found anywhere.
  - `scaled_rows` gives bit-identical values to the old division, from subnormal to 1e300.
  - Every STFT column matches the complex FFT of its window, for even and odd `nfft`, with and without overlap.
- **Comparison with `main`:** I ran the full suite on `main` (in a temporary worktree with its own target directory) and on the branch, both with `--nocapture`, and compared the error logs line by line.
  - The worst DOA errors are identical in every test.
  - Only 22 relative errors against the pyMUSIC golden spectra differ, at rounding level. For example, bin 14 went from 7.9e-8 to 5.2e-8.
  - The largest relative error is unchanged at 2.6e-5, against a tolerance of 1e-4.
  - The snapshot checks pass at 1e-9.

## Speed

Same machine and harness, `main` vs branch, 1 s recording:

| Workload | main | branch |
|---|---:|---:|
| IFB, 1 bin | 1123 µs | **532 µs** (−53%) |
| IFB, 80 bins | 4171 µs | **3161 µs** (−24%) |
| Narrowband | 1038 µs | **887 µs** (−15%) |

Most of what's left in the one-bin case is computing the STFT for all 81 bins. It has to: the silence check compares the requested bin against the strongest one in the whole spectrum. Getting clearly ahead of numpy would mean changing how that check works.

I haven't re-run the committed benchmark (`bench/results`, the README charts). `bench/README.md` says to re-run all three implementations after a change to musicrs; that takes about 12 minutes and needs the pyMUSIC and pySoundToolbox clones. Makes the preprocessing in `ifb_music_spectrum` (and the shared input handling of the narrowband path and `select_bins_by_energy`) cheaper. A one-bin IFB call was slower than the vectorized numpy baseline because about 85% of its time went into preprocessing the samples, not into MUSIC.

## Changes

- **One vectorizable pass for the input check and scaling** (`26d068e`): `ifb_music_spectrum` and `select_bins_by_energy` threw away the maximum that `check_real_samples` returns and computed it again with `data.amax()`. Both were single running `f64::max` loops, which the compiler cannot vectorize. `check_real_samples` now keeps eight independent lanes, and `scaled_rows` scales the data by a power of two and splits it into channels in one pass. Multiplying by the reciprocal of a power of two gives exactly the same values as dividing by it.
- **Real FFT for the STFT** (`c048b47`): it uses the cached `real_fft_plan` and reuses one buffer for all windows, instead of a complex FFT with a new buffer per window. `stft_with` and its planner parameter are gone.
- **Covariance per bin without allocations** (`51e7277`): each entry of the lower triangle is summed over the windows in the same order as before and mirrored into the upper triangle, instead of allocating vectors and a 4×4 matrix for every window.

## Speed

Same machine (Intel N150), 1 s recording, `main` vs this branch:

| Workload | main | branch |
|---|---:|---:|
| IFB, 1 bin | 1123 µs | 532 µs (−53%) |
| IFB, 80 bins | 4171 µs | 3161 µs (−24%) |
| Narrowband | 1038 µs | 887 µs (−15%) |

The numpy baseline in `bench/results` is 552 µs for one bin. `bench/results` and the README charts have **not** been re-run yet.

## Testing

- `cargo test -- --include-ignored`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` pass after each commit.
- New unit tests:
  - NaN, +inf and −inf are caught in every lane and in the leftover samples; the maximum is found wherever it is.
  - `scaled_rows` is bit-identical to division, from subnormal values up to 1e300.
  - STFT columns match the complex FFT of each window for even and odd `nfft`, with and without overlap.
- Compared `--nocapture` logs of the full suite on `main` and on this branch:
  - The worst DOA errors are identical in every test.
  - Only the relative errors against the pyMUSIC golden spectra differ, at rounding level. The largest is unchanged at 2.6e-5, against a tolerance of 1e-4.
  - The snapshot checks pass at 1e-9.

# CLAUDE.md

## Project Overview

**musicrs** is a Rust port of the MUSIC (MUltiple SIgnal Classification) algorithm for Direction-of-Arrival (DOA) estimation with microphone/antenna arrays. Based on R. O. Schmidt's 1986 algorithm and the Python pyMUSIC implementation.

## Commands

```bash
# Build
cargo build
cargo build --release

# Test
cargo test              # all tests except slow ones (#[ignore = "slow"])
cargo test -- --include-ignored   # full suite, including slow tests (CI runs this)
cargo test --lib        # unit tests only
cargo test --test '*'   # integration tests only
cargo test --test golden_test   # parity with the original pyMUSIC spectra
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings   # CI runs this and `cargo fmt --check`
cargo audit             # RustSec advisories in Cargo.lock (CI runs this; install cargo-audit first)

# Documentation
cargo doc --open
```

## Architecture

```
src/
├── lib.rs      # Public API exports and crate-level docs
├── error.rs    # MusicError (returned by every fallible public function) and `musicrs::error::Result` (not re-exported at the root)
├── music.rs    # Core MUSIC algorithm (MusicEstimator, spectrum, DOA estimation)
└── stft.rs     # Signal processing (STFT, analytic signal via Hilbert transform)
tests/
├── common/mod.rs                # Shared WAV/filename/angle helpers, ErrorLog
├── integration_test.rs          # Narrowband DOA on every WAV recording (±0.5°)
├── ifb_test.rs                  # IFB-MUSIC on the tone's bin (nfft 160), below Nyquist (±0.5°); repeated and reordered bins
├── errors_test.rs               # Every MusicError the public API returns
├── golden_test.rs               # Spectra vs. pyMUSIC (incl. partial interval, 2 sources narrowband and IFB, nfft 320/1024); analytic signal vs. scipy; musicrs snapshots at/above Nyquist
├── broadband_test.rs            # IFB-MUSIC on composite multi-tone signals; two sources at different angles
├── noisy_data_test.rs           # Narrowband and IFB (energy-selected bins) DOA with added white noise
├── synthetic_test.rs            # Synthetic plane waves: 2-D arrays, 2–3 sources, coherent sources (not resolved), endfire, edge cases, 48 kHz
├── golden/                      # pyMUSIC reference CSVs, *.musicrs.csv snapshots, generate_golden.py
└── data/single-source/*.wav     # 4-channel 24-bit 16kHz test recordings
examples/bench_pymusic.rs        # musicrs side of the runtime benchmark vs pyMUSIC
bench/                           # pyMUSIC and vectorized-numpy harnesses, analyze.py (stats + charts), results/; see bench/README.md
docs/benchmark*.svg              # charts shown in the README (light and dark), generated by bench/analyze.py
```

**Key types:**
- `MusicEstimator` — main struct; configure antenna positions, angle search range/step, sample rate, and number of sources
- `MusicEstimator::estimate_doa_from_real()` — real-data entry point (removes each channel's mean, then the covariance of the analytic signals, eigendecomposition, spectrum and peaks as in `estimate_doa`, without calling it), like pyMUSIC's `getSourceAngles`. It never forms the analytic signals: their covariance comes from each channel's real FFT by Parseval (`analytic_covariance`), with real FFT plans cached per thread (`stft::real_fft_plan`). The golden/snapshot spectrum tests build their covariance with `analytic_signal` instead, so they do not cover this path; only the DOA-level tests do
- `MusicEstimator::ifb_music_spectrum()` — wideband variant; bin frequencies use the estimator's `sample_rate`, so tones above Nyquist cannot be recovered
- `select_bins_by_energy()` — picks the IFB bins within N dB of the strongest; with `bins = None` noise-only bins dominate the geometric mean
- `analytic_signal()` — converts real signal to complex via Hilbert transform (FFT-based)
- `stft()` — Short-Time Fourier Transform with configurable window and overlap

- `MusicError` — bad data (wrong row count or covariance shape, no samples, NaN/inf, silence) and bad parameters (too many or zero sources, angle grid incl. spans over 2π, frequency ≤ 0 or non-finite, sample rate, antenna positions, `nfft`, overlap, threshold, no usable bins) are returned as `Err`; the public API does not panic on them and does not return a quiet wrong answer. The estimator's fields are checked where they are used, not in `new()`, because the fields are public. `noise_subspace` reads only the lower triangle of `cov`; IFB never uses the DC bin

**Core algorithm flow:**
1. Compute covariance matrix of complex multichannel input
2. Hermitian eigendecomposition (`faer`) → signal/noise subspace split
3. Compute MUSIC pseudo-spectrum using steering vectors
4. Peak detection → DOA estimates in radians

## Dependencies

| Crate | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| `nalgebra` | Matrix types and linear algebra |
| `num-complex` | Complex number arithmetic |
| `rustfft` | FFT for STFT and Hilbert transform |
| `realfft` | Real-input FFT for the narrowband covariance |
| `faer` | Numerically stable Hermitian eigendecomposition |
| `hound` (dev) | Reading WAV test fixtures |
| `approx` (dev) | Floating-point approximate equality in tests |

## Testing

Integration tests load WAV files from `tests/data/single-source/` and compare DOA estimates with the ground truth in the file name. Clean recordings land exactly on the true angle, so their tolerance is one 0.5° grid step; noisy and broadband-triple tests use tolerances set a little above the measured worst error. `common::ErrorLog` prints the worst error per test (`cargo test -- --nocapture`), which is the number to re-check before changing a tolerance. File naming convention:

```
single-source_<freq>Hz_<doa>deg_<duration>s.wav
```

Test data covers:
- Frequencies: 300 Hz – 9.1 kHz (in ~1.1 kHz steps)
- Angles: 0°, 40°, 80°, 120°, 160°
- Durations: 1 s and 2 s
- Array: Kinect 4-mic geometry

## Workflow

- Before implementing a non-trivial change, propose a plan and get it approved first. While planning, ask clarifying questions about anything ambiguous (scope, API shape, defaults, test data) rather than guessing.

- Make changes on a branch, never directly on `main`:
  - `feat/<feature-name>` for new features
  - `fix/<bugfix-name>` for bug fixes
- Structure work in reasonably sized commits: each commit is one logical change that builds and passes tests on its own.
- A project Stop hook (`.claude/settings.json` → `.claude/hooks/run-tests.sh`) runs `cargo test` when a turn ends with changed code under `src/`, `tests/` or `Cargo.*`, and sends failures back to Claude. Tests that take more than ~10 s are marked `#[ignore = "slow"]`, so the hook skips them; run `cargo test -- --include-ignored` for the full suite. Set `MUSICRS_SKIP_HOOK_TESTS=1` before starting Claude Code to turn the hook off.
- Parallel builds (subagents in separate worktrees, or a second `cargo test` next to the Stop hook) must not share a Cargo target directory. Worktrees of this crate produce the same test-binary paths (e.g. `target/debug/deps/noisy_data_test-<hash>`), and cargo releases its build lock before running the tests, so one run can execute another worktree's binary: tests go missing or fail on code that isn't there, or a binary being rewritten fails with "Permission denied". Give each worktree its own `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` (on this 3-core machine also `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=1`), and check that new tests appear by name in the output before trusting a run.

## Notes

- Rust edition 2024, MSRV follows current stable toolchain
- No `rustfmt.toml` or `clippy.toml` — use `cargo fmt` and `cargo clippy` defaults
- Golden files: `*.eigh.csv` (pyMUSIC with `np.linalg.eigh`) and `*.hilbert_n<N>.scipy.csv` (`scipy.signal.hilbert`) must match value-by-value; `*.eig.csv` (pyMUSIC as published) only by peak location, because `np.linalg.eig` returns a non-orthogonal noise basis on this near-noiseless data. Regenerate with the command in `tests/golden/generate_golden.py`.
- Snapshot files: `*.narrowband.musicrs.csv` in `tests/golden/` are musicrs's own narrowband spectra at and above Nyquist (8000 Hz, 9100 Hz), not pyMUSIC references (musicrs deliberately differs from pyMUSIC there). They pin the at/above-Nyquist steering-vector behaviour: `1 / spectrum` (the MUSIC denominator) must match to 1e-9 of its maximum and the peak must not move. The spectrum itself is not compared relatively, because at the peaks its denominator is at rounding level and moves with the eigensolver. After an intended change, regenerate with `MUSICRS_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1 cargo test --test golden_test` and review the diff.
- Sign convention: musicrs uses a non-conjugated analytic signal with an `exp(+j2πfτ)` steering vector; pyMUSIC conjugates the analytic signal and uses `exp(−j2πfτ)`. Equivalent below Nyquist. The above-Nyquist sign flip and the real steering vector at Nyquist are musicrs additions tuned to the test data.

content.text:
All three review points were valid. I fixed each in its own commit, pushed them to PR #35, and replied in each comment thread. The full suite still passes, including the slow tests, along with clippy and fmt. I didn't wait for CI on the new commits.

1. **Minimum Rust version** (`631b354`): I set `rust-version = "1.89"`, not the 1.88 the review suggested. `nalgebra` 0.35, which `main` already uses, needs Rust 1.89. So the crate didn't build on 1.85–1.88 even before this PR; `Cargo.toml` just didn't say so. I installed both toolchains to check: the tests pass on Rust 1.89, and Rust 1.88 is now rejected with a clear version message. I also updated the minimum-version note in `CLAUDE.md`.
2. **Plan cache in `stft`** (`ac56873`): the `stft` docs now say that FFT plans for the last 4 transform lengths are kept per thread, and hold their memory until they're evicted or the thread exits.
3. **Covariance test** (`6abc8bd`): the per-bin loop is now its own function, `cross_spectral_matrix`. A unit test checks that it gives bit-for-bit the same matrix as the old sum of outer products, for several microphone and window counts. A swapped index or a missing conjugate would fail it directly.

The review's fourth point, the out-of-date benchmark results, is still open; the PR description says so too. I can re-run the full benchmark on this branch (about 12 minutes, needs the pyMUSIC and pySoundToolbox clones) if you want the numbers updated before merging.

## Performance vs pyMUSIC and numpy

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="docs/benchmark-dark.svg">
  <img alt="Dot plot of mean time per call on a log scale, with p5 to p95 lines, for pyMUSIC, a vectorized numpy implementation of the same algorithm, and musicrs. pyMUSIC takes 146 to 164 ms per call, and 11.63 s for IFB-MUSIC over 80 bins. musicrs is 3.03 and 2.05 times faster than vectorized numpy for narrowband DOA (1.08 ms vs 3.28 ms, 2.66 ms vs 5.47 ms) and 3.94 times faster for IFB-MUSIC over 80 bins (4.75 ms vs 18.7 ms), but 2.12 and 2.33 times slower for single-bin IFB-MUSIC (1.17 ms vs 552 µs). It is 61 to 2,447 times faster than pyMUSIC." src="docs/benchmark.svg">
</picture>

The same calls on the same recordings (1400 Hz, 40°), from the real-valued samples to the
result, in three implementations:

- **pyMUSIC**, run unmodified;
- **numpy (vectorized)**, pyMUSIC's algorithm written the way numpy is meant to be used
  ([`bench/bench_numpy.py`](bench/bench_numpy.py)): the same analytic signal,
  `np.linalg.eig` and steering vectors, but in `float64`, with all 720 angles in one array
  operation, on one thread. Before timing, its spectra are checked against pyMUSIC's (relative
  difference below 1e-7, same peak), and for narrowband DOA also the covariance, built with
  pySoundToolbox's analytic signal as pyMUSIC does;
- **musicrs**, single-threaded.

**Against pyMUSIC, musicrs is 61× to 2,447× faster, but that is not a Rust-vs-Python
result.** Almost all of pyMUSIC's time goes to a Python loop that builds the 720 steering
vectors one element at a time in software-emulated `float128`, with `np.matrix` products.
That loop costs ~145–165 ms per pseudo-spectrum whatever the recording length, and IFB-MUSIC
needs one spectrum per bin. Written idiomatically, the same algorithm in numpy takes
milliseconds.

**Against vectorized numpy, musicrs is 2.0× to 3.0× faster on narrowband DOA and 3.9× faster
on IFB-MUSIC over 80 bins, but 2.1× to 2.3× slower on single-bin IFB-MUSIC.**

- *Narrowband* never forms the analytic signals. Their covariance is computed directly from
  each channel's real FFT (Parseval's theorem), so there is no inverse FFT and no complex
  N-sample matrix, and the FFT plans are reused between calls. numpy does a complex FFT and an
  inverse FFT per channel and then a matrix product over all samples.
- *IFB-MUSIC over 80 bins* is dominated by the per-bin work of 80 eigendecompositions and 80
  spectra. numpy pays Python and call overhead for each bin.
- *Single-bin IFB-MUSIC* hasn't been optimised yet. musicrs computes the STFT and the power of
  every bin, then uses only one of them. It has not been profiled.

The same calls on the same recordings (1400 Hz, 40°), from the real-valued samples to the
result, in three implementations:

result.** Almost all of pyMUSIC's time goes to a Python loop that builds the 720 steering
vectors one element at a time in software-emulated `float128`, with `np.matrix` products.

needs one spectrum per bin. Written idiomatically, the same algorithm in numpy takes
milliseconds.

Before timing, its spectra are checked against pyMUSIC's (relative difference below 1e-7, same peak), and for narrowband DOA also the covariance, built with pySoundToolbox's analytic signal as pyMUSIC does; - **musicrs**, single-threaded. **Against pyMUSIC, musicrs is 61× to 2,447× faster, but that is not a Rust-vs-Python result.** Almost all of pyMUSIC's time goes to a Python loop that builds the 720 steering vectors one element at a time in software-emulated `float128`, with `np.matrix` products. That loop costs ~145–165 ms per pseudo-spectrum whatever the recording length, and IFB-MUSIC needs one spectrum per bin. Written idiomatically, the same algorithm in numpy takes milliseconds. **Against vectorized numpy, musicrs is 2.0× to 3.0× faster on narrowband DOA and 3.9× faster on IFB-MUSIC over 80 bins, but 2.1× to 2.3× slower on single-bin IFB-MUSIC.** - *Narrowband* never forms the analytic signals. txt = txt.slice(0, sStart) + `- **Scheduling moves the mean by a few percent.** The mean is at most 3.8 % above the median,
  and the outliers (calls slower than median + 3 robust sigmas) raise the mean by at most
  2.8 % (*tail excess*). No call takes more than 1.71× the median of its case, so mean and
  median are both fair single numbers; they give the same ratios to within 3 %. Because the
  distributions are skewed, ± stddev overstates the spread below the mean; the p5 – p95
  column shows the real range.
- **Slow calls come in runs.** Lag-1 autocorrelation is 0.4 to 0.8, so neighbouring calls are
  alike. Isolated preemptions would hit calls independently; runs point to slower changes in
  machine state (CPU frequency, caches, the core the process runs on). pyMUSIC on single-bin
  IFB-MUSIC (2 s recording) also drifted: its last 10 % of calls were 12 % slower than its
  first.
- **Run to run**, numpy's means moved by up to 3.4 % and pyMUSIC's by up to 4.8 % against the
  run the day before; earlier comparisons gave up to 9 %. Read the numbers as about ± 20 %.
  The ratios between musicrs and numpy on narrowband DOA and on 80 bins (2.6× to 6.3×) are
  larger than that, and the ratios to pyMUSIC far larger. On single-bin IFB-MUSIC the two are
  level within that margin.

` + txt.slice(sEnd);
await write(R, txt);
await write('bench/results/environment.txt', (await file('bench/results/environment.txt').text())
  .replace(/^musicrs: .*$/m, `musicrs: ${SHA} (bench/ changes aside, the code the results were measured on)`)
  .replace(/^rustc .*$/m, (await $`rustc --version`.text()).trim())
  .replace(/^Date: .*$/m, 'Date: 2026-11-24'));
(await $`git diff --stat && git diff bench/results/environment.txt && sed -n 55,62p README.md | cut -c1-200 && sed -n 118,135p README.md`.text())

file.content:
# musicrs Rust implementation of MUltiple SIgnal Classification (MUSIC), described by R. O. Schmidt ([paper](http://ieeexplore.ieee.org/xpl/articleDetails.jsp?arnumber=1143830)), for Direction-of-Arrival (DOA) estimation with microphone arrays. It is a port of [pyMUSIC](https://github.com/amjadsaadeh/pyMUSIC), the implementation written for empirical investigations of MUSIC in my master thesis. Pure Rust, no LAPACK. ## Features - Narrowband MUSIC: covariance → noise subspace (Hermitian eigendecomposition via `faer`) → pseudo-spectrum `1 / ‖Eₙᴴ a(θ)‖²` → peak picking. - Multi-source peak picking (circular local maxima, highest first). pyMUSIC's `getSourceAngles` clustered all estimates around the first peak; this is fixed here. - IFB-MUSIC (wideband): per-bin cross-spectral matrices from an STFT, narrowband spectra combined by geometric mean. - FFT-based analytic signal (Hilbert transform) and STFT helpers. ## Usage ```rust use musicrs::MusicEstimator; use nalgebra::DMatrix; // Default: Kinect 4-mic linear array, 720 angle steps over [0, 2π), 16 kHz let estimator = MusicEstimator::default(); // 4 × N real-valued microphone samples, e.g. read from a WAV file let data: DMatrix = /* ... */; // Narrowband DOA of one 1400 Hz source, in radians let angles = estimator.estimate_doa_from_real(&data, 1, 1400.0)?; // Wideband: IFB-MUSIC spectrum over chosen STFT bins (nfft = 160 → 100 Hz bins) let (spectrum, angles) = estimator.ifb_music_spectrum(&data, 160, 1, Some(&[14]))?; ``` Bad input (wrong channel count, NaN, silence, too many sources, an unusable angle grid, …) is returned as a `MusicError`. For other arrays use `MusicEstimator::new(antenna_positions, angle_steps_num, search_interval, sample_rate)` with `[x, y]` positions in metres. If you already have complex (analytic) data, call `estimate_doa` directly. ### Things to keep in mind - A linear array cannot distinguish θ from 360° − θ; restrict `search_interval` to [0, π] if you want a single answer. - IFB-MUSIC only sees frequencies up to Nyquist (`sample_rate / 2`); a tone recorded above Nyquist is aliased and its DOA cannot be recovered from the STFT bins. - Running IFB-MUSIC over *all* bins on a narrowband signal is dominated by noise-only bins; select the bins that carry signal energy. ## Performance vs pyMUSIC and numpy The same calls on the same recordings (1400 Hz, 40°), from the real-valued samples to the result, in three implementations: - **pyMUSIC**, run unmodified; - **numpy (vectorized)**, pyMUSIC's algorithm written the way numpy is meant to be used ([`bench/bench_numpy.py`](bench/bench_numpy.py)): the same analytic signal, `np.linalg.eig` and steering vectors, but in `float64`, with all 720 angles in one array operation, on one thread. Before timing, its spectra are checked against pyMUSIC's (relative difference below 1e-7, same peak), and for narrowband DOA also the covariance, built with pySoundToolbox's analytic signal as pyMUSIC does; - **musicrs**, single-threaded. **Against pyMUSIC, musicrs is 61× to 2,447× faster, but that is not a Rust-vs-Python result.** Almost all of pyMUSIC's time goes to a Python loop that builds the 720 steering vectors one element at a time in software-emulated `float128`, with `np.matrix` products. That loop costs ~145–165 ms per pseudo-spectrum whatever the recording length, and IFB-MUSIC needs one spectrum per bin. Written idiomatically, the same algorithm in numpy takes milliseconds. **Against vectorized numpy, musicrs is 2.0× to 3.0× faster on narrowband DOA and 3.9× faster on IFB-MUSIC over 80 bins, but 2.1× to 2.3× slower on single-bin IFB-MUSIC.** - *Narrowband* never forms the analytic signals. Their covariance is computed directly from each channel's real FFT (Parseval's theorem), so there is no inverse FFT and no complex N-sample matrix, and the FFT plans are reused between calls. numpy does a complex FFT and an inverse FFT per channel and then a matrix product over all samples. - *IFB-MUSIC over 80 bins* is dominated by the per-bin work of 80 eigendecompositions and 80 spectra. numpy pays Python and call overhead for each bin. - *Single-bin IFB-MUSIC* hasn't been optimised yet. musicrs computes the STFT and the power of every bin, then uses only one of them. Schmidt ([paper](http://ieeexplore.ieee.org/xpl/articleDetails.jsp?arnumber=1143830)), for Direction-of-Arrival (DOA) estimation with microphone arrays. It is a port of [pyMUSIC](https://github.com/amjadsaadeh/pyMUSIC), the implementation written for empirical investigations of MUSIC in my master thesis. Pure Rust, no LAPACK. ## Features - Narrowband MUSIC: covariance → noise subspace (Hermitian eigendecomposition via `faer`) → pseudo-spectrum `1 / ‖Eₙᴴ a(θ)‖²` → peak picking. - Multi-source peak picking (circular local maxima, highest first). pyMUSIC's `getSourceAngles` clustered all estimates around the first peak; this is fixed here. - IFB-MUSIC (wideband): per-bin cross-spectral matrices from an STFT, narrowband spectra combined by geometric mean. - FFT-based analytic signal (Hilbert transform) and STFT helpers. ## Usage ```rust use musicrs::MusicEstimator; use nalgebra::DMatrix; // Default: Kinect 4-mic linear array, 720 angle steps over [0, 2π), 16 kHz let estimator = MusicEstimator::default(); // 4 × N real-valued microphone samples, e.g. read from a WAV file let data: DMatrix = /* ... */; // Narrowband DOA of one 1400 Hz source, in radians let angles = estimator.estimate_doa_from_real(&data, 1, 1400.0)?; // Wideband: IFB-MUSIC spectrum over chosen STFT bins (nfft = 160 → 100 Hz bins) let (spectrum, angles) = estimator.ifb_music_spectrum(&data, 160, 1, Some(&[14]))?; ``` Bad input (wrong channel count, NaN, silence, too many sources, an unusable angle grid, …) is returned as a `MusicError`. For other arrays use `MusicEstimator::new(antenna_positions, angle_steps_num, search_interval, sample_rate)` with `[x, y]` positions in metres. If you already have complex (analytic) data, call `estimate_doa` directly. ### Things to keep in mind - A linear array cannot distinguish θ from 360° − θ; restrict `search_interval` to [0, π] if you want a single answer. - IFB-MUSIC only sees frequencies up to Nyquist (`sample_rate / 2`); a tone recorded above Nyquist is aliased and its DOA cannot be recovered from the STFT bins. - Running IFB-MUSIC over *all* bins on a narrowband signal is dominated by noise-only bins; select the bins that carry signal energy. ## Performance vs pyMUSIC and numpy The same calls on the same recordings (1400 Hz, 40°), from the real-valued samples to the result, in three implementations: - **pyMUSIC**, run unmodified; - **numpy (vectorized)**, pyMUSIC's algorithm written the way numpy is meant to be used ([`bench/bench_numpy.py`](bench/bench_numpy.py)): the same analytic signal, `np.linalg.eig` and steering vectors, but in `float64`, with all 720 angles in one array operation, on one thread. # musicrs Rust implementation of MUltiple SIgnal Classification (MUSIC), described by R. O. Schmidt ([paper](http://ieeexplore.ieee.org/xpl/articleDetails.jsp?arnumber=1143830)), for Direction-of-Arrival (DOA) estimation with microphone arrays. It is a port of [pyMUSIC](https://github.com/amjadsaadeh/pyMUSIC), the implementation written for empirical investigations of MUSIC in my master thesis. Pure Rust, no LAPACK. ## Features - Narrowband MUSIC: covariance → noise subspace (Hermitian eigendecomposition via `faer`) → pseudo-spectrum `1 / ‖Eₙᴴ a(θ)‖²` → peak picking. - Multi-source peak picking (circular local maxima, highest first). pyMUSIC's `getSourceAngles` clustered all estimates around the first peak; this is fixed here. - IFB-MUSIC (wideband): per-bin cross-spectral matrices from an STFT, narrowband spectra combined by geometric mean. - FFT-based analytic signal (Hilbert transform) and STFT helpers. ## Usage ```rust use musicrs::MusicEstimator; use nalgebra::DMatrix; // Default: Kinect 4-mic linear array, 720 angle steps over [0, 2π), 16 kHz let estimator = MusicEstimator::default(); // 4 × N real-valued microphone samples, e.g. read from a WAV file let data: DMatrix = /* ... */; // Narrowband DOA of one 1400 Hz source, in radians let angles = estimator.estimate_doa_from_real(&data, 1, 1400.0)?; // Wideband: IFB-MUSIC spectrum over chosen STFT bins (nfft = 160 → 100 Hz bins) let (spectrum, angles) = estimator.ifb_music_spectrum(&data, 160, 1, Some(&[14]))?; ``` Bad input (wrong channel count, NaN, silence, too many sources, an unusable angle grid, …) is returned as a `MusicError`. For other arrays use `MusicEstimator::new(antenna_positions, angle_steps_num, search_interval, sample_rate)` with `[x, y]` positions in metres. If you already have complex (analytic) data, call `estimate_doa` directly. ### Things to keep in mind - A linear array cannot distinguish θ from 360° − θ; restrict `search_interval` to [0, π] if you want a single answer. - IFB-MUSIC only sees frequencies up to Nyquist (`sample_rate / 2`); a tone recorded above Nyquist is aliased and its DOA cannot be recovered from the STFT bins. - Running IFB-MUSIC over *all* bins on a narrowband signal is dominated by noise-only bins; select the bins that carry signal energy. ## Performance vs pyMUSIC and numpy The same calls on the same recordings (1400 Hz, 40°), from the real-valued samples to the result, in three implementations: - **pyMUSIC**, run unmodified; - **numpy (vectorized)**, pyMUSIC's algorithm written the way numpy is meant to be used ([`bench/bench_numpy.py`](bench/bench_numpy.py)): the same analytic signal, `np.linalg.eig` and steering vectors, but in `float64`, with all 720 angles in one array operation, on one thread. Before timing, its spectra are checked against pyMUSIC's (relative difference below 1e-7, same peak), and for narrowband DOA also the covariance, built with pySoundToolbox's analytic signal as pyMUSIC does; - **musicrs**, single-threaded. **Against pyMUSIC, musicrs is 79× to 3,904× faster, but that is not a Rust-vs-Python result.** Almost all of pyMUSIC's time goes to a Python loop that builds the 720 steering vectors one element at a time in software-emulated `float128`, with `np.matrix` products. That loop costs ~150–165 ms per pseudo-spectrum whatever the recording length, and IFB-MUSIC needs one spectrum per bin. Written idiomatically, the same algorithm in numpy takes milliseconds. **Against vectorized numpy, musicrs is 2.6× to 3.5× faster on narrowband DOA and 6.3× faster on IFB-MUSIC over 80 bins, and level on single-bin IFB-MUSIC (1.16× on the 1 s recording, 1.00× on the 2 s one).** - *Narrowband* never forms the analytic signals. Their covariance is computed directly from each channel's real FFT (Parseval's theorem), so there is no inverse FFT and no complex N-sample matrix, and the FFT plans are reused between calls. numpy does a complex FFT and an inverse FFT per channel and then a matrix product over all samples. - *IFB-MUSIC over 80 bins* is dominated by the per-bin work of 80 eigendecompositions and 80 spectra. numpy pays Python and call overhead for each bin. - *Single-bin IFB-MUSIC* is mostly preprocessing, not MUSIC: checking and scaling the samples and the STFT of every bin. The silence check compares the requested bin with the strongest bin of the whole spectrum, so all bins are computed. file.content:
Makes the preprocessing in `ifb_music_spectrum` (and the shared input handling of the narrowband path and `select_bins_by_energy`) cheaper. A one-bin IFB call was slower than the vectorized numpy baseline because about 85% of its time went into preprocessing the samples, not into MUSIC.

## Changes

- **One vectorizable pass for the input check and scaling** (`26d068e`): `ifb_music_spectrum` and `select_bins_by_energy` threw away the maximum that `check_real_samples` returns and computed it again with `data.amax()`. Both were single running `f64::max` loops, which the compiler cannot vectorize. `check_real_samples` now keeps eight independent lanes, and `scaled_rows` scales the data by a power of two and splits it into channels in one pass. Multiplying by the reciprocal of a power of two gives exactly the same values as dividing by it.

I re-ran the full benchmark on `6abc8bd`, committed the results as `7ed79ce` and pushed them to PR #35. I also updated the PR description with the new numbers and the review follow-ups. The three implementations ran one after the other on this machine. Before timing, the numpy harness checked its results against pyMUSIC, and all agreed.

| Workload | musicrs | numpy | musicrs vs numpy | musicrs vs pyMUSIC |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Narrowband · 1 s | 966 µs | 3.38 ms | 3.50× | 168× |
| Narrowband · 2 s | 2.08 ms | 5.29 ms | 2.55× | 79× |
| IFB, 1 bin · 1 s | 485 µs | 563 µs | **1.16×** (was 0.47×) | 316× |
| IFB, 1 bin · 2 s | 889 µs | 891 µs | **1.00×** (was 0.43×) | 171× |
| IFB, 80 bins · 1 s | 3.01 ms | 19.0 ms | 6.30× (was 3.94×) | 3,904× |

Single-bin IFB-MUSIC went from about twice as slow as numpy to level with it. Separate runs vary by up to about 20%, so the 1.16× lead on the 1 s recording is within that margin.

Changes in the commit:
- **Results:** `bench/results` (the raw timings, summaries and `environment.txt`) and the four charts in `docs/`. `environment.txt` now records `6abc8bd` and rustc 1.100; the earlier runs used 1.88, which the README now notes.
- **README:**
  - The main results table and the distribution statistics are replaced with the new ones.
  - The summary sentences are updated, and the single-bin IFB-MUSIC paragraph now explains where its time goes.
  - "musicrs over time" has a new `6abc8bd` column and an entry describing what changed.
  - The text on the timing distributions is rewritten. The groups of very slow musicrs calls from the last run are gone: no call took more than 1.71× the median of its workload.

To run the benchmark I cloned pyMUSIC and pySoundToolbox at the pinned commits into the scratchpad, at `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-orchid-projects-musicrs/46911313-2cca-4da2-9c13-85365306ce52/scratchpad/ext`. I also installed the Rust 1.88 and 1.89 toolchains with rustup for the minimum-version check. You can remove them with `rustup toolchain uninstall 1.88 1.89` if you don't need them.

    fn steering_vector_into(&self, angle: f64, frequency: f64, out: &mut [Cplx]) {
        let dir = [angle.cos(), angle.sin()];
        // For f < Nyquist (sr/2): analytic signal has positive phase → use +exponent.
        // For f > Nyquist: signal aliases in the one-sided FFT; dominant eigenvector
        // phase is conjugated → use −exponent.
        // At exactly Nyquist (f == sr/2): analytic signal is real; noise subspace is
        // also real → use cos(phase) as a real steering vector.
        let nyquist = self.sample_rate / 2.0;
        let phase_sign = if frequency > nyquist {
            -1.0_f64
        } else {
            1.0_f64
        };
        let at_nyquist = (frequency - nyquist).abs() < 0.5;
        for (element, p) in out.iter_mut().zip(&self.antenna_positions) {
            let delay = (p[0] * dir[0] + p[1] * dir[1]) / SPEED_OF_SOUND;
            let phase = phase_sign * 2.0 * PI * frequency * delay;
            *element = if at_nyquist {
                // Real steering vector: imaginary part is zero
                Cplx::new(phase.cos(), 0.0)
            } else {
                Cplx::from_polar(1.0, phase)
            };
        }
    }
    pub fn spectrum(&self, noise_mat: &CMatrix, frequency: f64) -> Result<(Vec<f64>, Vec<f64>)> {
        self.check_rows(noise_mat.nrows())?;
        self.check_array()?;
        Self::check_frequency(frequency)?;
        let angles = self.angle_grid()?;
        let mut a = vec![Cplx::new(0.0, 0.0); self.n_antennas()];
        let scores: Vec<f64> = angles
            .iter()
            .map(|&theta| {
                self.steering_vector_into(theta, frequency, &mut a);
                // ‖Eₙᴴ a‖²: one inner product per noise eigenvector (column of noise_mat)
                let denom: f64 = noise_mat
                    .column_iter()
                    .map(|e| {
                        e.iter()
                            .zip(&a)
                            .map(|(e, a)| e.conj() * a)
                            .sum::<Cplx>()
                            .norm_sqr()
                    })
                    .sum();
                if denom == 0.0 {
                    f64::INFINITY
                } else {
                    1.0 / denom
                }
            })
            .collect();

        Ok((scores, angles))
    }

fn hermitian_eigen(mat: &CMatrix) -> (Vec<f64>, CMatrix) {
    use faer::{Mat as FaerMat, Side, c64};

    let n = mat.nrows();

    // Convert nalgebra complex matrix → faer complex matrix
    let faer_mat: FaerMat<c64> = FaerMat::from_fn(n, n, |i, j| {
        let c = mat[(i, j)];
        c64::new(c.re, c.im)
    });

    // Numerically stable Hermitian eigendecomposition. It only fails to converge on
    // non-finite input, which every caller rejects first.
    let evd = faer_mat
        .self_adjoint_eigen(Side::Lower)
        .expect("Hermitian eigendecomposition of a finite matrix converges");

    // Eigenvalues are real but stored as c64 with im ≈ 0; extract via .re
    let s_col = evd.S().column_vector();
    let u_mat = evd.U();

    // faer documents its eigenvalues as nondecreasing; sort anyway so the ascending
    // order this function promises does not depend on that.
    let mut order: Vec<usize> = (0..n).collect();
    order.sort_unstable_by(|&a, &b| s_col[a].re.total_cmp(&s_col[b].re));

    let eigenvalues: Vec<f64> = order.iter().map(|&i| s_col[i].re).collect();
    // Copy the eigenvectors (reordered by ascending eigenvalue) back into nalgebra.
    // faer's eigenvectors already satisfy A·v = λ·v, so no conjugation is applied;
    // the steering-vector sign convention in `steering_vector` is matched to this.
    let eigenvectors: CMatrix = CMatrix::from_fn(n, n, |row, col| {
        let src_col = order[col];
        let c = u_mat[(row, src_col)];
        Cplx::new(c.re, c.im)
    });

    (eigenvalues, eigenvectors)
}
fn find_peaks(scores: &[f64], angles: &[f64], n: usize, circular: bool) -> Vec<f64> {
    let len = scores.len();
    if len == 0 || n == 0 {
        return Vec::new();
    }

    // Runs of equal scores as inclusive index ranges.
    let mut runs: Vec<(usize, usize)> = Vec::new();
    let mut run_start = 0;
    for i in 1..=len {
        if i == len || scores[i] != scores[run_start] {
            runs.push((run_start, i - 1));
            run_start = i;
        }
    }
    if runs.len() == 1 {
        // A single point on an open range has no neighbours, so it is a peak (as for
        // `angle_steps_num = 1`); a longer constant spectrum has none.
        return if len == 1 && !circular {
            vec![angles[0]]
        } else {
            Vec::new()
        };
    }
    // On the circle, a run at the start continues the run at the end. Its indices then
    // go past `len` and are taken modulo `len`.
    if circular && scores[0] == scores[len - 1] {
        let (_, first_end) = runs.remove(0);
        runs.last_mut().unwrap().1 = first_end + len;
    }

    let score = |i: usize| scores[i % len];
    let midpoint = |(a, b): (usize, usize)| {
        if b < len {
            (angles[a] + angles[b]) / 2.0
        } else {
            let step = angles[1] - angles[0];
            let mid = (a + b) as f64 / 2.0;
            if mid >= len as f64 {
                angles[0] + step * (mid - len as f64)
            } else {
                angles[a] + step * (mid - a as f64)
            }
        }
    };

    let r = runs.len();
    let mut peaks: Vec<(f64, f64)> = (0..r)
        .filter_map(|k| {
            let (a, b) = runs[k];
            let prev = match k {
                0 if circular => Some(score(runs[r - 1].1)),
                0 => None,
                _ => Some(score(runs[k - 1].1)),
            };
            let next = match k + 1 {
                j if j < r => Some(score(runs[j].0)),
                _ if circular => Some(score(runs[0].0)),
                _ => None,
            };
            let v = score(a);
            (prev.is_none_or(|p| v > p) && next.is_none_or(|q| v > q))
                .then(|| (v, midpoint((a, b))))
        })
        .collect();

    peaks.sort_unstable_by(|a, b| b.0.total_cmp(&a.0));
    peaks.into_iter().take(n).map(|(_, a)| a).collect()
}
    pub fn noise_subspace(&self, cov: &CMatrix, n_sources: usize) -> Result<CMatrix> {
        let n = self.n_antennas();
        if cov.shape() != (n, n) {
            return Err(MusicError::CovarianceShape {
                n_antennas: n,
                rows: cov.nrows(),
                cols: cov.ncols(),
            });
        }
        self.check_sources(n_sources)?;
        if !cov.iter().all(|c| c.re.is_finite() && c.im.is_finite()) {
            return Err(MusicError::NonFiniteData);
        }

        // Eigenvectors in ascending eigenvalue order; the first n_noise columns are the
        // noise subspace (smallest eigenvalues).
        let (_eigenvalues, eigenvectors) = hermitian_eigen(cov);
        let n_noise = cov.nrows() - n_sources;
        Ok(eigenvectors.columns(0, n_noise).into())
    }
